name: Nora Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, forty-three, an electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I wire houses and repair shop circuits, mostly the ordinary jobs rather than anything exotic. I use AI every day to draft customer messages and compare parts lists, but I take my own measurements and check the actual fittings before trusting a list.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like away from the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ben maintains gardens, and our children are eleven and fourteen. We have a mortgage, about twenty-two days of expenses saved and my lower-than-usual wage for an electrician; only a few other electrical firms are nearby. I like trying a tool before the others have heard of it, but I still do the Sunday roast from my mother's handwritten recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say useful is enough; a tool doesn't have to change civilisation to help me finish a message. I'd tell the owner which subscriptions actually save time and which ones we can drop. A small firm should spend money on what works, not what makes a good photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the household money even if the AI story quietens down. Twenty-two days saved doesn't give us much room if Ben has a bad weather month or my shifts fall. I can be quick with software and still be badly paid for the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the repair shifts now and throughout the first year, using the AI message tool daily but checking every detail myself. I'd ask the owner next month for a pay review with three finished jobs showing the time I saved. At home we'd cancel the meal-delivery subscription and use the difference for current bills rather than sign up for another work tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bank account and still interested in the day. I don't need to choose between liking a new tool and wanting the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show in the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The before-and-after time on messages, with the electrical checks left exactly as thorough. I'd ask for a specific weekly rise, not claim a fast reply makes me the best electrician in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop using the tool if the rise was refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a tool I find useful, but I'd stop volunteering extra unpaid office work. Saving ten minutes doesn't mean I have offered the owner my evening for free.

say: I think **useful small tools** are worthwhile without changing the whole world.
I'd tell the owner to pay for **what works**, rather than subscriptions chosen for a photograph.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, with a mortgage and twenty-two days of expenses saved.
My **quick software use** does not protect us if gardening income or my paid shifts fall.
do: Keep **repair shifts** and check daily AI customer messages myself now and through the first year.
Request a **pay review** next month using three finished jobs with measured message-time savings.
Cancel the **meal-delivery subscription** and use the difference for current household bills.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, enjoying a tool without confusing that with financial security.
S0.quote: Saving ten minutes doesn't mean I have offered the owner my evening for free.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive habits** appear in daily tools and measured examples, while she remains an ordinary experienced electrician rather than a specialist.
Cancelling **meal delivery** supports current bills; the same money is not also counted as new savings or a technology budget.

steps.text: Keep the home and shop repair shifts
Cancel meal delivery to help cover current household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small contractor should try the tools and compete, but be honest about what has actually improved. I'd offer to test the new quoting assistant during paid hours. I wouldn't tell customers we have a magic price when the wall hasn't even been opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could be squeezed if the owner uses quicker planning to promise more work for the same small wage. Most of my day is physical repair, so I don't think AI alone takes the whole job. I worry about losing paid time at the edges, which still matters when the savings cover only twenty-two days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd offer a four-week paid quoting trial, keeping my normal repair pay and checking every result against completed jobs. In the first year I'd show the owner actual time and material errors before agreeing to use it on customer quotes. Ben and I would postpone replacing our working garden shed while we see whether paid hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but keen to put a real tool through a real test. The frightening bit is a wage changing without anybody saying clearly what changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you show the owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quote that assumes a clear cable route where we spent an hour getting behind a fitted cabinet. I'd keep the customer's name out of the comparison. I wouldn't leave an hour of real repair work out to make the tool look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the shed decision release?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred we have not committed. The roof is sound, so we can put up with the sticky door rather than turn the emergency account into a building project.

say: I'd favour **tested competition**, with honest claims about what a quoting tool actually improves.
I'd offer **paid trials** rather than promise customers a magic price before checking the building.
think: My **paid time could shrink** if quicker planning becomes more work for the same low wage.
Physical repair should continue, but **small hour cuts** still matter with only twenty-two days saved.
do: Offer a **four-week paid trial** with normal repair pay kept and results checked against finished jobs.
Show **time and material errors** before agreeing to use the assistant for customer quotes.
Delay the **six-hundred shed replacement** while paid hours remain uncertain.
feel: **Anxious and curious**, wanting a real test before accepting a wage change hidden in new targets.
S1.quote: I wouldn't leave an hour of real repair work out to make the tool look good.
fieldNote: She **tests early** but requires paid trial time and retained repair pay, preventing enthusiasm from becoming an offer of free office labour.
The **shed spending** is uncommitted and cosmetic while the roof remains sound, making postponement a feasible budget choice.

steps.text: Trial the quoting assistant for four paid weeks with normal repair pay retained
Postpone the uncommitted six-hundred shed replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031. I'd ask the owner which paid work we can still sell at each stage, rather than demand a comforting slogan. I'd prefer a paid route into different equipment over a lecture about why I should be optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big drop in my hours when robots can do ordinary fitting around 2031 and larger firms take more of our customers. Ben's gardening could face robots too, even if both of us still have awkward physical jobs for a while. Twenty-two days saved isn't enough to cover a long gap in both wages, and I'd still have the mortgage at forty-eight unless something else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd apply to advertised building-equipment service posts, but only where the written wage covers travel and our bills and training is paid. I'd keep this job until a signed offer, not resign because I like the sound of a course. We'd ask my parents about specific emergency childcare if one of us needs an interview or paid class, and I'd contact the lender to compare hardship terms and total costs before agreeing to help. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs while seeking those signed, affordable service offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even while I'm searching. I like a risk I can test; I don't like a mortgage gap I can't fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents be able to cover every interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask about particular days and accept that they may say no. They're family, not a childcare service waiting for my timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment servicing if robots can learn that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd compare real paid work available at the time, not call any title safe forever. I need a route that pays for a real week, while admitting the route might change again.

say: I'd ask what **paid work** remains at each stage, thinking AI in 2028 and robots around 2031.
I'd prefer **paid equipment training** over a comforting slogan or a lecture about optimism.
think: I expect **a big hours drop** when robots reach ordinary fitting around 2031 and larger firms win customers.
Ben's **gardening work** could also face robots, leaving a twenty-two-day reserve against a possible household wage gap.
do: Apply for **advertised service work** with written wages covering bills and travel, paid training, and current work retained until a signed offer.
Ask my parents about **specific emergency childcare**, without assuming availability.
Compare the lender's **hardship terms** and total mortgage costs before agreeing to anything.
feel: **Alarmed but searching**, willing to test a job offer while lacking money for a long mortgage gap.
S2.quote: I like a risk I can test; I don't like a mortgage gap I can't fund.
fieldNote: Her **expected hours loss** follows physical robots around 2031, while earlier thinking changes affect planning rather than instantly performing electrical repairs.
Family help and **lender options** remain conditional enquiries, and another service post is not treated as permanent protection from automation.

steps.text: Seek posted service offers covering bills/travel with paid training, keeping current work until signed
Ask my parents about specific emergency childcare days
Compare lender hardship terms and total mortgage costs before agreeing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a firm train people while the repair work still pays. I'd ask for a proper paid apprenticeship-style place on the new equipment. I don't care about an impressive certificate if nobody can name a task I'll be paid to do afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could fall, but five years lets me check a practical route before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I can't treat retirement as something already waiting for me. I can learn quickly, but I can't create the fee or a missed week's wage by being enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for a paid class in control-system fault finding, enrolling only with the employer paying fees and keeping my full weekly wage. I'd require supervised practice on working equipment, not just a screen exercise. In the first year after 2031 I'd use the new planning tools on paid jobs while checking them against real sites, and save thirty-five monthly only after essentials are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to choose than in the quick picture. I can picture practising after a sensible paid lesson instead of buying a course at midnight because a headline frightened me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer pays the fee but cuts your ordinary shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask for the full weekly pay to be written into the agreement before enrolling. An unchanged hourly rate doesn't feed the family if half the hours disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the thirty-five unavailable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A necessary school cost, a mortgage rise or a repair we can't put off. I'd lower the target rather than borrow to prove I can save.

say: I'd ask employers for **paid practical places** while existing repair work still brings money in.
I'd want training to name **actual paid tasks**, rather than rely on an impressive certificate.
think: My **income could fall**, but five years gives me time to check a practical route before 2031.
My **quick learning** does not pay course fees or replace wages missed while training.
do: Enrol in **practical control training** only with employer-paid fees, written full weekly pay protection and supervised practice on working equipment.
Check new **planning tools** against real sites on paid jobs after 2031.
Save **thirty-five monthly** only after essential household bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious but selective**, able to compare a paid practical route without a rushed purchase.
S3.quote: An unchanged hourly rate doesn't feed the family if half the hours disappear.
fieldNote: Her **paid training** requires full weekly wages, working equipment and supervised practice, rather than assuming daily AI use supplies an equipment qualification.
The **saving target** yields to necessary costs, so she neither borrows to maintain it nor spends the emergency reserve twice.

steps.text: Enrol only with employer-paid fees, written full weekly pay protection and supervised practice on working equipment
Save thirty-five monthly only after essential bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children should see different work before deciding what to study, rather than inherit my fears or my trade. I'd ask the school about free work visits in areas they choose. I'd still favour paid apprenticeships for adults who need to change while paying a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our low pay and short reserve worry me now, even if thinking AI waits until 2036. I'll be fifty-three then and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039; the children will be twenty-one and twenty-four at the thinking date. I don't know the remaining mortgage or whether either child will need help, so I can't spend their imagined independence today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue the same fully paid practical class now and keep the conditional thirty-five saving plan. This year I'd ask the school about free work visits chosen around the children's interests. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual service vacancies if my hours fall, taking a post only with affordable signed pay terms and paid learning for equipment I don't yet know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household budget, but less hurried by the technology. I can enjoy trying a new tool without pretending I have to choose the children's whole future this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot with a decade to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to know the full price and see real paid demand. I don't have those figures or spare money now. I won't buy a robot without prices, customers and maintenance costs I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a child wants to follow your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd arrange a proper visit and explain that I like the work, including what is uncertain. I wouldn't call it safe for life just because the practical tasks last longer than the paperwork.

say: I'd seek **varied free work visits** rather than let the children inherit my trade or my fears.
I'd favour **paid adult apprenticeships** for people learning while they still owe a mortgage.
think: Our low pay and **short reserve** worry me now despite the longer technological warning.
I cannot assume **adult children** need no support or that the mortgage is cleared when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Enrol in **practical control training** only with employer-paid fees, written full weekly pay protection and supervised practice on working equipment.
Ask the school for **free work visits** around the children's interests.
Compare **actual service vacancies** after cuts, requiring affordable signed pay terms and paid learning for unfamiliar equipment.
feel: **Anxious about money**, but less hurried by the distant change and curious about useful tools.
S4.quote: I won't buy a robot without prices, customers and maintenance costs I can afford.
fieldNote: She **advances family ages** correctly without treating grown children or an assumed cleared mortgage as income available to solve present bills.
A possible **future robot purchase** remains outside action tags because she lacks prices, customers, affordable maintenance and spare capital.

steps.text: Enrol only with employer-paid fees, written full weekly pay protection and supervised practice on working equipment
Save thirty-five monthly only after essential bills are paid
Ask the school about free work visits in fields the children choose
Compare service offers after 2036 hour cuts, requiring affordable signed wages and paid learning before leaving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because ordinary fitting could face robots around 2031 before we've built a real financial cushion. Paid practical training with my full weekly wage protected would help. I want a real offer of work and learning, not a course I have to pay for by missing a mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether enjoying new tools means a person has money to buy a new life. I can test a message-writing tool on my phone tonight; I can't test not paying the mortgage and undo it in the morning. Curiosity is something I have, not money the bank accepts.

headlineQuote: Curiosity is something I have, not money the bank accepts.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and licence, doing ordinary home wiring and shop repairs.
She has **twenty-two days saved**, low pay, few nearby employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with gardening-worker husband Ben.
She uses **AI daily**, likes testing early and favours practical paid work, while respecting her family's time and limited resources.
She is **already anxious** about money; fast AGI alarms her, and every training or job plan keeps full-pay and affordability conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring physical robots around 2031 before the household builds a meaningful financial cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** must protect full weekly wages, with fees covered and real working equipment.
A **real paid-work offer** would help more than an unfunded course that risks the mortgage.
